Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

exFuelGrowth.title: Retail sales ex fuel vs fuel sales growth
exFuelGrowth.content:
Retail sales ex fuel is total revenue with the volatile fuel line stripped out -- the closest proxy in the disclosure to Kroger's identical/comparable-store sales growth, since fuel swings on the retail gas price rather than store traffic or basket size. Fuel sales growth is shown alongside it for contrast.

For The Kroger Co.: a quarter where blended Revenue growth looks weak (or strong) but ex-fuel growth is steady is a fuel-price effect, not a change in the grocery business; management's own guidance is framed on the ex-fuel number.

What to watch:

  • Ex-fuel growth decelerating even though fuel is a tailwind (the real top-line signal)
  • Fuel growth diverging sharply from ex-fuel growth -- a sign the blended Revenue chart above is being distorted by gas prices

ecommerce.title: Digital / e-commerce sales growth
ecommerce.content:
E-commerce sales growth is the YoY growth rate of Kroger's digital channel -- pickup, delivery and ship-to-home -- disclosed separately from in-store retail sales.

For The Kroger Co.: digital is management's stated growth engine against a low-single-digit ex-fuel physical-store trend, and funds the delivery/fulfilment capex also visible in the CapEx chart below.

What to watch:

  • Digital growth decelerating toward the ex-fuel store rate (the engine stalling)
  • Whether digital growth is still outrunning the capex it requires to sustain fulfilment capacity

fuelSales.title: Fuel sales
fuelSales.content:
Fuel sales is revenue from Kroger's fuel centers, reported as a distinct line because it moves almost entirely with the retail price of gasoline rather than gallons sold.

For The Kroger Co.: fuel sales fell every year from FY2024 (-12.3%) through FY2026 (-9.3%) on lower pump prices even as ex-fuel retail sales grew -- the gap is why the blended Revenue chart understates the grocery business's actual trajectory in a falling-fuel-price year.

What to watch:

  • Fuel sales direction driven by gas prices, not demand -- read it as a headline-revenue offset, not an operating signal
  • Fuel gross margin (not shown) typically moves opposite to the retail price swing

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For The Kroger Co.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For The Kroger Co.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For The Kroger Co.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For The Kroger Co.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For The Kroger Co.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For The Kroger Co.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For The Kroger Co.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For The Kroger Co.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For The Kroger Co.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For The Kroger Co.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

dcf.base_sublabel: Owner FCF — after SBC, interest income & leases
dcf.model_approach_note: One fix pass, 2026-11-15. No driver or value change: the trip is a denominator artifact (GAAP EPS 1.54 after the 2.5bn fulfilment-network impairment vs 4.85 adjusted; the actual trailing P/E was already 51.6x). Fix 1 (mid-cycle FCF) tested and recorded as inputs.mid_cycle_fcf = 2,373 (mid-point of median 1,447 and latest 3,299 owner FCF): base year-1 levered owner FCF is ~2.0bn, already below it, because the component build never compounds from last_fcf. Fix 2 (WACC premium): 7.5% already carries ~1.1 points over the computed ~6.4%, now itemised in wacc_rationale; not raised. Fix 3 (growth cap): base 1.8-2.5% vs 5-year revenue CAGR 2.2%. Fix 4 (exit cap): base terminal value 7.2x EBITDA vs 10-year average 7.9x. Passing the rule would need a base value <= ~50.8 (about 5.7x EV/adjusted EBITDA, below the 10-year minimum of 6.0x). Recorded as a known false positive; expected to clear when fiscal 2026 EPS replaces the impaired year. Detail in valuation_philosophy.sanity_check_response.
